content: A study conducted between 1988 and 1997 examined 246,371 children, of whom 177,304 were included in the analysis. Overweight in 4-year-old children was defined as having a BMI-for-age above the 95th percentile based on the 2000 CDC growth reference, while underweight was defined as a BMI-for-age below the 5th percentile. A sub-analysis included 12,587 mother-child pairs, depending on the availability of pregnancy records. Exclusion criteria included children without breastfeeding duration data, inconsistent breastfeeding reports, or missing data on height, weight, gender, race/ethnicity, and birth weight. Breastfeeding duration was categorized into six groups: never, 1 month, 1–2 months, 3–5 months, 6–11 months, and 12 months or more. The CARDIA study, a U.S. multicenter prospective cohort study, examined cardiovascular disease risk trends in young Black and White men and women. Participants were recruited from four geographic areas: Birmingham, Alabama; Chicago, Illinois; Minneapolis, Minnesota; and Oakland, California. Exclusion criteria included diabetes, hysterectomy, oophorectomy, pregnancy, or lactation at baseline, as well as missing lactation duration data. Women reported lactation duration for all births, categorized into less than 6 weeks, 6–11 weeks, 3–6 months, or 6 months or more. Lactation duration was calculated as the midpoint of each category and summed across all births. A cross-sectional study in South Australia involved 448 pregnant women identifying as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. The study assessed the impact of dental care interventions during pregnancy, fluoride varnish application, anticipatory guidance, and motivational interviewing on early childhood caries (ECC) prevalence at 24 and 36 months. Breastfeeding duration was divided into four categories: never, less than 12 months, 12–23 months, and 24 months or longer. ECC was defined as the presence of at least one decayed, missing, or filled tooth at 3 years of age. A retrospective cohort study in Myanmar examined mothers of 25–30-month-old children. Data were collected on nursing, dietary, and oral hygiene habits. ECC was defined as the presence of caries in at least one tooth, diagnosed through visual examination and probing. Children consuming jaggery (a caramel sugar) were excluded from further analysis. The Southampton Women’s Survey (SWS) in the UK followed children born to non-pregnant women aged 20–34 years. Breastfeeding duration was recorded based on the date of the last breastfeed. Dietary data were collected at 6 and 12 months using food frequency questionnaires administered by trained nurses. The NHANES survey (1999–2002) analyzed data from 1,576 children aged 2–5 years. Breastfeeding history and duration were categorized as overall, full, or exclusive breastfeeding. Dental examinations were conducted to assess oral health outcomes. The CASPIAN-III study in Iran included 5,528 students aged 10–18 years. Breastfeeding duration was divided into five categories: 0 months, less than 6 months, 6–12 months, 12–18 months, and 18–24 months. The Korean National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) study followed postmenopausal women aged 40 and older. The primary outcome was newly diagnosed lung cancer, defined by ICD-10 codes. Participants were followed from one year after their health check-up until lung cancer diagnosis, death, or the study's end. The Child Development Supplement (CDS) of the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) collected data on 3,271 children and their families. Breastfeeding duration was grouped into four categories: never, less than 6 months, 7–12 months, and more than 12 months. Cognitive and behavioral outcomes were assessed. The China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) collected longitudinal data on breastfeeding duration, as recalled by parents, to examine its impact on child development. This summary provides a clear and professional overview of the studies, their methodologies, and key findings.
